17	  Abstract
18	  The aponeurosis is a large fibrous connective tissue structure within and surrounding skeletal muscle
19	  and is a critical component of the muscle–tendon unit (MTU). Due to the lack of consensus on terminology
20	  and the heterogeneous nature of the aponeurosis between MTUs, there are several questions that remain
21	  unanswered. For example, the aponeurosis is often conflated with the free tendon rather than being consid-
22	  ered an independent structure. This has subsequent implications when interpreting data regarding the struc-
23	  ture, function, and adaptation of the aponeuroses from these studies. In recent years, a body of work
24	  has emerged to suggest that acute injury to the myo-aponeurotic complex may have an impact on return-to-
25	  sport timeframes and reinjury rates. Therefore, the purpose of this review is to provide a more detailed under-
26	  standing of the morphology and mechanical behaviour common to all aponeuroses, as well as the unique
27	  characteristics of specific lower-limb aponeuroses that are commonly injured. This review provides the prac-
28	  titioner with a current understanding of the mechanical, material, and adaptive properties of lower limb
29	  aponeuroses and suggests directions for future research related to the myo-aponeurotic complex.
30	
31	  Key points
32	
33	     1. In the current body of literature, there is inconsistency in the terminology and classification used to describe
34	        and study aponeuroses. This has subsequent implications when interpreting data regarding specific aponeurotic
35	        structures.
36	     2. Injuries to the MTU also commonly involve damage or disruption to the aponeurosis and these injuries have
37	        often been associated with longer return-to-play times and have higher rates of re-injury compared to isolated
38	        muscle injuries
39	     3. For clinicians it is important to understand the structure, function, and adaptive properties of aponeuroses as this
40	        may provide motivation for future research to direct myo-aponeurotic injury rehabilitation and prevention strate‑
41	        gies.

The Structure, Function, and Adaptation
of Lower‑Limb Aponeuroses: Implications
for Myo‑Aponeurotic Injury
Scott Hulm1,2* , Ryan G. Timmins1,2, Jack T. Hickey2,3, Nirav Maniar1,2, Yi‑Chung Lin1,2, Katherine R. Knaus4,
Bryan C. Heiderscheit5, Silvia S. Blemker6 and David A. Opar1,2



  Abstract
  The aponeurosis is a large fibrous connective tissue structure within and surrounding skeletal muscle
  and is a critical component of the muscle–tendon unit (MTU). Due to the lack of consensus on terminology
  and the heterogeneous nature of the aponeurosis between MTUs, there are several questions that remain
  unanswered. For example, the aponeurosis is often conflated with the free tendon rather than being consid-
  ered an independent structure. This has subsequent implications when interpreting data regarding the struc-
  ture, function, and adaptation of the aponeuroses from these studies. In recent years, a body of work
  has emerged to suggest that acute injury to the myo-aponeurotic complex may have an impact on return-to-
  sport timeframes and reinjury rates. Therefore, the purpose of this review is to provide a more detailed under-
  standing of the morphology and mechanical behaviour common to all aponeuroses, as well as the unique
  characteristics of specific lower-limb aponeuroses that are commonly injured. This review provides the prac-
  titioner with a current understanding of the mechanical, material, and adaptive properties of lower limb
  aponeuroses and suggests directions for future research related to the myo-aponeurotic complex.

  Key points

     1. In the current body of literature, there is inconsistency in the terminology and classification used to describe
        and study aponeuroses. This has subsequent implications when interpreting data regarding specific aponeurotic
        structures.
     2. Injuries to the MTU also commonly involve damage or disruption to the aponeurosis and these injuries have
        often been associated with longer return-to-play times and have higher rates of re-injury compared to isolated
        muscle injuries
     3. For clinicians it is important to understand the structure, function, and adaptive properties of aponeuroses as this
        may provide motivation for future research to direct myo-aponeurotic injury rehabilitation and prevention strate‑
        gies.

  Keywords Aponeurosis, Muscle–tendon injury, Morphology, Mechanical behaviour, Remodelling

716	                                        7. Practical Considerations and Periodization Strategies
717	                                              Strategic planning, periodization, and recovery are crucial for optimizing HIIT’s im-
718	                                        pact on strength and power development. While HIIT effectively enhances neuromuscular
719	                                        efficiency, power, and endurance, improper integration with strength training can cause
720	                                        fatigue accumulation and interference, impeding long-term gains. Balancing HIIT with
721	                                        traditional strength training and tailoring protocols to individual needs are essential for
722	                                        maximizing performance adaptations.
723	
724	                                        7.1. Balancing HIIT with Strength Training
725	                                             Integrating HIIT with strength training requires strategic planning to minimize in-
726	                                        terference effects and optimize strength and power gains. Short-duration, high-intensity
727	                                        efforts in HIIT can enhance neuromuscular activation, particularly when combined with
728	                                        blood-flow restriction, which has been shown to improve sprint performance and anaero-
729	                                        bic adaptations without significantly affecting cardiorespiratory fitness [16]. HIIT should
730	                                        moderate volume and intensity to prevent excessive fatigue, especially during competition
731	                                        phases [75]. Scheduling HIIT separately from or after strength training maximizes force
732	                                        production during resistance exercises, minimizing fatigue-related impairments [75]. Addi-
733	                                        tionally, managing lower-body intensive HIIT is essential to prevent overloading muscle
734	                                        groups involved in resistance training, with adequate recovery being crucial to avoiding
735	                                        interference effects [76].
736	 Life 2025, 15, 657                                                                                            13 of 19
737	
738	
739	
740	                     7.2. Fatigue Management and Recovery Strategies
741	                          HIIT is a potent stimulus for physiological adaptation but also imposes significant
742	                     neuromuscular fatigue. Heart Rate Variability (HRV) and Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE)
743	                     are adequate for assessing recovery status, with HRV providing insights into autonomic
744	                     recovery and RPE indicating perceived exertion levels [77]. Neuromuscular fatigue can be
745	                     evaluated through CMJ and grip strength tests, with CMJ performance typically declining
746	                     post-exercise and recovering within 48–72 h [78]. Active recovery methods, such as alter-
747	                     nating hot and cold water immersion, enhance blood flow, reduce muscle soreness, and
748	                     expedite recovery [77]. Nutritional strategies, including adequate protein and carbohydrate
749	                     intake, support muscle repair and glycogen replenishment, while hydration and quality
750	                     sleep are critical for hormonal recovery and neuromuscular efficiency [79]. HIIT induces
751	                     central and peripheral fatigue, impacting neural function and muscle contractility. Yet,
752	                     when managed correctly, it significantly enhances aerobic capacity and performance metrics
753	                     such as VO2 max and repeated-sprint ability [21,25,80,81].
754	
755	                     7.3. Individualization of HIIT Protocols
756	                           Effectively optimizing HIIT for strength and power development depends on tailoring
757	                     protocols to the individual athlete’s profile, including their training history, current physical
758	                     condition, and specific performance goals. Lower-intensity HIIT with longer recovery suits
759	                     beginners, while elite athletes benefit from high-intensity protocols with shorter recoveries
760	                     that simulate competition [45]. Sport-specific adaptations are also essential; resistance-based
761	                     HIIT can enhance strength under fatigue for contact sports, while sprint and plyometric
762	                     HIIT effectively improve RFD and acceleration for speed-based sports [45,82]. Adjusting
763	                     work-to-rest ratios based on sport-specific demands is essential. For example, high work-to-
764	                     rest ratios (1:3 or greater) favor recovery and power output in sprint protocols, while lower
765	                     ratios (1:1 or 2:1) can enhance metabolic conditioning and fatigue resistance. Individual
766	                     responses to these ratios should guide HIIT design, particularly for optimizing strength,
767	                     hypertrophy, or reactive power. Individualizing HIIT using metrics like anaerobic speed
768	                     reserve (ASR) and anaerobic power reserve (APR) has been shown to promote uniform
769	                     physiological adaptations among athletes with diverse profiles [83,84]. Integrating HIIT with
770	                     strength training can further enhance aerobic fitness and match performance, underscoring
771	                     the importance of a comprehensive approach [85]. Periodized HIIT, adjusted for intensity,
772	                     volume, and recovery, maximizes neuromuscular adaptations and minimizes injury risk,
773	                     supporting sustained performance improvements [26,86].
774	                           Strategic HIIT periodization effectively maximizes neuromuscular adaptations while
775	                     preserving strength and power gains. Combining HIIT with strength training, implement-
776	                     ing effective fatigue management, and customizing protocols based on individual needs
777	                     can significantly enhance explosive performance, endurance, and injury resilience. When
778	                     applied thoughtfully, HIIT is a complementary approach to strength training, creating a
779	                     synergistic effect that optimizes long-term performance and power output. A detailed
780	                     overview of the key focus on HIIT practical considerations and periodization strategies is
781	                     presented in Table 5.

812	                                         8. Future Research Directions
813	                                               The long-term effects of HIIT on neuromuscular function, strength, and power remain
814	                                         insufficiently understood, as most studies emphasize short-term adaptations. Examining
815	                                         sustained improvements in maximal strength, power output, and muscle hypertrophy
816	                                         through extended HIIT protocols, in comparison to traditional resistance training, is cru-
817	                                         cial. Equally important is the investigation of potential risks associated with long-term
818	                                         HIIT application, including injury susceptibility, neuromuscular fatigue accumulation, and
819	                                         overtraining, especially when protocols are not adequately individualized or periodized.
820	                                         Additionally, assessing risks such as overuse injuries, neuromuscular fatigue, and adaptive
821	                                         plateaus could refine periodization strategies, ensuring that HIIT is implemented safely and
822	                                         effectively for power-dominant sports. Understanding individual variability in response to
823	                                         HIIT—shaped by genetics, muscle fiber composition, and training history—may allow for
824	                                         more personalized protocols that enhance power adaptations while minimizing fatigue and
825	                                         interference effects. In addition, the application of HIIT in children and adolescent athletes
826	                                         remains an understudied area. Considering the developmental differences in neuromuscu-
827	                                         lar systems and recovery profiles, future research should investigate age-appropriate HIIT
828	                                         protocols, neuromuscular outcomes, and safety implications in pediatric populations.
829	                                               Exploring optimal HIIT protocols for power-based sports like weightlifting, sprinting,
830	                                         and combat sports is also essential. Future research should also stratify findings based
831	                                         on HIIT methodology, including variations in work duration, rest intervals, and intensity
832	                                         levels. Differentiating these variables will allow a more precise understanding of how
833	                                         specific HIIT formats drive distinct neuromuscular adaptations. Evaluating the efficacy of
834	                                         sprint interval training (SIT), plyometric-integrated HIIT, and resistance-based HIIT could
835	                                         provide more precise guidelines for maximizing power output. Integrating HIIT with
836	                                         traditional strength, hypertrophy, and plyometric training requires careful consideration to
837	                                         avoid interference effects. With appropriate adjustments to HIIT intensities, frequencies,
838	                                         and work-to-rest ratios, strategic periodization may help maintain strength gains while
839	                                         enhancing power. Future research should also explore monitoring tools and recovery
840	                                         strategies that support the safe and sustainable implementation of HIIT over the long term.
841	                                         Advancing these research areas can provide valuable insights for coaches and athletes,
842	                                         ensuring that HIIT is a powerful tool for sustainable improvements in strength, power, and
843	                                         overall performance.
844	 Life 2025, 15, 657                                                                                                                 15 of 19
845	
846	
847	
848	                                  9. Conclusions
849	                                       High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) has proven to be a versatile and effective
850	                                  method for enhancing neuromuscular function, strength, power, and endurance. Its ability
851	                                  to optimize motor unit recruitment, muscle fiber composition, and neuromuscular efficiency
852	                                  underscores its value for power-based and intermittent sports. Maximizing the benefits of
853	                                  HIIT while minimizing potential interference effects with traditional resistance training
854	                                  requires careful planning, periodization, and individualized programming. Strategic
855	                                  integration of HIIT with strength, hypertrophy, and plyometric training can result in
856	                                  comprehensive improvements in explosive force production, fatigue resistance, and overall
857	                                  athletic performance. Continued research into HIIT’s long-term effects, individualized
858	                                  responses, and optimal protocols will further refine its application in high-performance
859	                                  training programs, enabling athletes to achieve sustainable gains in strength, power, and
860	                                  sport-specific abilities.

                                        7. Practical Considerations and Periodization Strategies
                                              Strategic planning, periodization, and recovery are crucial for optimizing HIIT’s im-
                                        pact on strength and power development. While HIIT effectively enhances neuromuscular
                                        efficiency, power, and endurance, improper integration with strength training can cause
                                        fatigue accumulation and interference, impeding long-term gains. Balancing HIIT with
                                        traditional strength training and tailoring protocols to individual needs are essential for
                                        maximizing performance adaptations.

                                        7.1. Balancing HIIT with Strength Training
                                             Integrating HIIT with strength training requires strategic planning to minimize in-
                                        terference effects and optimize strength and power gains. Short-duration, high-intensity
                                        efforts in HIIT can enhance neuromuscular activation, particularly when combined with
                                        blood-flow restriction, which has been shown to improve sprint performance and anaero-
                                        bic adaptations without significantly affecting cardiorespiratory fitness [16]. HIIT should
                                        moderate volume and intensity to prevent excessive fatigue, especially during competition
                                        phases [75]. Scheduling HIIT separately from or after strength training maximizes force
                                        production during resistance exercises, minimizing fatigue-related impairments [75]. Addi-
                                        tionally, managing lower-body intensive HIIT is essential to prevent overloading muscle
                                        groups involved in resistance training, with adequate recovery being crucial to avoiding
                                        interference effects [76].

                     7.2. Fatigue Management and Recovery Strategies
                          HIIT is a potent stimulus for physiological adaptation but also imposes significant
                     neuromuscular fatigue. Heart Rate Variability (HRV) and Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE)
                     are adequate for assessing recovery status, with HRV providing insights into autonomic
                     recovery and RPE indicating perceived exertion levels [77]. Neuromuscular fatigue can be
                     evaluated through CMJ and grip strength tests, with CMJ performance typically declining
                     post-exercise and recovering within 48–72 h [78]. Active recovery methods, such as alter-
                     nating hot and cold water immersion, enhance blood flow, reduce muscle soreness, and
                     expedite recovery [77]. Nutritional strategies, including adequate protein and carbohydrate
                     intake, support muscle repair and glycogen replenishment, while hydration and quality
                     sleep are critical for hormonal recovery and neuromuscular efficiency [79]. HIIT induces
                     central and peripheral fatigue, impacting neural function and muscle contractility. Yet,
                     when managed correctly, it significantly enhances aerobic capacity and performance metrics
                     such as VO2 max and repeated-sprint ability [21,25,80,81].

                     7.3. Individualization of HIIT Protocols
                           Effectively optimizing HIIT for strength and power development depends on tailoring
                     protocols to the individual athlete’s profile, including their training history, current physical
                     condition, and specific performance goals. Lower-intensity HIIT with longer recovery suits
                     beginners, while elite athletes benefit from high-intensity protocols with shorter recoveries
                     that simulate competition [45]. Sport-specific adaptations are also essential; resistance-based
                     HIIT can enhance strength under fatigue for contact sports, while sprint and plyometric
                     HIIT effectively improve RFD and acceleration for speed-based sports [45,82]. Adjusting
                     work-to-rest ratios based on sport-specific demands is essential. For example, high work-to-
                     rest ratios (1:3 or greater) favor recovery and power output in sprint protocols, while lower
                     ratios (1:1 or 2:1) can enhance metabolic conditioning and fatigue resistance. Individual
                     responses to these ratios should guide HIIT design, particularly for optimizing strength,
                     hypertrophy, or reactive power. Individualizing HIIT using metrics like anaerobic speed
                     reserve (ASR) and anaerobic power reserve (APR) has been shown to promote uniform
                     physiological adaptations among athletes with diverse profiles [83,84]. Integrating HIIT with
                     strength training can further enhance aerobic fitness and match performance, underscoring
                     the importance of a comprehensive approach [85]. Periodized HIIT, adjusted for intensity,
                     volume, and recovery, maximizes neuromuscular adaptations and minimizes injury risk,
                     supporting sustained performance improvements [26,86].
                           Strategic HIIT periodization effectively maximizes neuromuscular adaptations while
                     preserving strength and power gains. Combining HIIT with strength training, implement-
                     ing effective fatigue management, and customizing protocols based on individual needs
                     can significantly enhance explosive performance, endurance, and injury resilience. When
                     applied thoughtfully, HIIT is a complementary approach to strength training, creating a
                     synergistic effect that optimizes long-term performance and power output. A detailed
                     overview of the key focus on HIIT practical considerations and periodization strategies is
                     presented in Table 5.

                                         8. Future Research Directions
                                               The long-term effects of HIIT on neuromuscular function, strength, and power remain
                                         insufficiently understood, as most studies emphasize short-term adaptations. Examining
                                         sustained improvements in maximal strength, power output, and muscle hypertrophy
                                         through extended HIIT protocols, in comparison to traditional resistance training, is cru-
                                         cial. Equally important is the investigation of potential risks associated with long-term
                                         HIIT application, including injury susceptibility, neuromuscular fatigue accumulation, and
                                         overtraining, especially when protocols are not adequately individualized or periodized.
                                         Additionally, assessing risks such as overuse injuries, neuromuscular fatigue, and adaptive
                                         plateaus could refine periodization strategies, ensuring that HIIT is implemented safely and
                                         effectively for power-dominant sports. Understanding individual variability in response to
                                         HIIT—shaped by genetics, muscle fiber composition, and training history—may allow for
                                         more personalized protocols that enhance power adaptations while minimizing fatigue and
                                         interference effects. In addition, the application of HIIT in children and adolescent athletes
                                         remains an understudied area. Considering the developmental differences in neuromuscu-
                                         lar systems and recovery profiles, future research should investigate age-appropriate HIIT
                                         protocols, neuromuscular outcomes, and safety implications in pediatric populations.
                                               Exploring optimal HIIT protocols for power-based sports like weightlifting, sprinting,
                                         and combat sports is also essential. Future research should also stratify findings based
                                         on HIIT methodology, including variations in work duration, rest intervals, and intensity
                                         levels. Differentiating these variables will allow a more precise understanding of how
                                         specific HIIT formats drive distinct neuromuscular adaptations. Evaluating the efficacy of
                                         sprint interval training (SIT), plyometric-integrated HIIT, and resistance-based HIIT could
                                         provide more precise guidelines for maximizing power output. Integrating HIIT with
                                         traditional strength, hypertrophy, and plyometric training requires careful consideration to
                                         avoid interference effects. With appropriate adjustments to HIIT intensities, frequencies,
                                         and work-to-rest ratios, strategic periodization may help maintain strength gains while
                                         enhancing power. Future research should also explore monitoring tools and recovery
                                         strategies that support the safe and sustainable implementation of HIIT over the long term.
                                         Advancing these research areas can provide valuable insights for coaches and athletes,
                                         ensuring that HIIT is a powerful tool for sustainable improvements in strength, power, and
                                         overall performance.

                                  9. Conclusions
                                       High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) has proven to be a versatile and effective
                                  method for enhancing neuromuscular function, strength, power, and endurance. Its ability
                                  to optimize motor unit recruitment, muscle fiber composition, and neuromuscular efficiency
                                  underscores its value for power-based and intermittent sports. Maximizing the benefits of
                                  HIIT while minimizing potential interference effects with traditional resistance training
                                  requires careful planning, periodization, and individualized programming. Strategic
                                  integration of HIIT with strength, hypertrophy, and plyometric training can result in
                                  comprehensive improvements in explosive force production, fatigue resistance, and overall
                                  athletic performance. Continued research into HIIT’s long-term effects, individualized
                                  responses, and optimal protocols will further refine its application in high-performance
                                  training programs, enabling athletes to achieve sustainable gains in strength, power, and
                                  sport-specific abilities.

 "evidenceSummary": "Repeated-measures comparison of two linear velocity devices (GymAware PowerTool and Tendo Power Analyzer) in 14 resistance-trained men performing hang clean pulls at 20 to 140% of their 1RM hang power clean. The GymAware showed excellent reliability on all measures, and the Tendo showed excellent reliability for mean velocity at all loads, with peak velocity reliability falling from excellent at 20 to 80% to good at 100 and 120% and moderate at 140%.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 14 men, described as resistance-trained rather than as athletes, so results may not transfer to other groups. The GymAware was the criterion because 3D motion capture was unavailable, so neither device was checked against a gold standard.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read 'reliable and accurate' as 'interchangeable'; the authors state the devices should not be used interchangeably, and the Tendo showed proportional bias at 140% 1RM, with fixed bias for peak velocity at that load.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Kissick CR, Techmanski BS, Comfort P, Suchomel TJ. The Reliability, Bias, Differences, and Agreement Between Velocity Measurement Devices During the Hang Clean Pull. J Strength Cond Res. 2025;39(3):289-294.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "Fourteen resistance-trained men performed hang clean pulls at 20 to 140% of their 1RM hang power clean while wearing a GymAware PowerTool and a Tendo Power Analyzer. The study compared reliability, bias, and the size of differences in mean and peak barbell velocity between the two devices.",
  "tldr": "Both devices give reliable barbell velocity data for the hang clean pull up to 140% 1RM, but the Tendo is less reliable for peak velocity at heavy loads. The two devices should not be swapped, since the Tendo read 4 to 7% higher on mean velocity.",
  "methods": "Fourteen resistance-trained men (88.3 kg) completed three hang clean pulls at each of seven loads with both devices attached to the barbell. Reliability was assessed with ICC and CV%, bias with least-products regression, and effect sizes with Hedges g, using the GymAware as the criterion device.",
  "findings": "The GymAware had excellent reliability on all measures. The Tendo had excellent reliability for mean velocity at all loads and for peak velocity at 20 to 80% 1RM, good at 100 and 120%, and moderate at 140%. The Tendo showed proportional bias for mean and peak velocity at 140% 1RM and fixed bias for peak velocity at that load; effect sizes were small and the authors judged the differences not practically meaningful.",
  "limitations": "Small sample of resistance-trained men, not described as athletes. The GymAware was the criterion device because 3D motion capture was unavailable. Lifting straps were used at 100 to 140%. The authors suggest the Tendo's failure to account for horizontal bar displacement may explain the heavy-load drop in reliability.",
  "practicalImplications": "Either device can track barbell velocity in the hang clean pull, but the two should not be used interchangeably. Peak velocity from the Tendo should be read with caution above 80% 1RM. Keeping one device for a given lifter across a training block is the safer approach.",
  "athleteDev": "Use one velocity device per lifter across a block and do not compare numbers between devices. Treat heavy-load peak velocity from the Tendo as less certain.",
  "rtp": "Not a return-to-sport study, and it included no injured or rehabilitating participants. It cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or judge rehabilitation progress."

{
 "id": "Q18",
 "sourceFile": "The Risk Factors of Hamstring Strain Injury Induced by High-Speed Running.pdf",
 "decision": "DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "The article's own DOI is not printed in the extracted text. Operator to verify externally; all other fields are filled.",
 "doiMissing": true,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'The Risk Factors of Hamstring Strain Injury Induced by High-Speed Running' in the text matches the filename; journal header Journal of Sports Science and Medicine (2018) 17, 650-655.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Case-control Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Track & Field"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Collegiate", "Healthy Athletes", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Prospective nested case-control study of 61 male track and field athletes (sprinters, long jumpers and decathletes) followed through one competitive season, with 18 athletes who sustained hamstring strain injuries during high-speed running matched to 18 uninjured controls. Preseason isokinetic hip and knee strength, muscle thickness, range of motion and hamstring tightness did not differ significantly between groups, and the only significant factor was a previous hamstring injury (injury ratio 25.0% in legs with a history vs 10.5% without; OR 2.85).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 18 injury cases from one collegiate team, so power is low and the non-significant results cannot rule out associations. Injury history was obtained by questionnaire, and the tests may lack specificity to sprint running, as the authors acknowledge.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may over-read the injury-history odds ratio (OR 2.85) as a strong predictor, or read the hip range-of-motion trend (p = 0.064 and 0.095, not significant) as a real finding, when this is a small, single-team observational study.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Tokutake G, Kuramochi R, Murata Y, Enoki S, Koto Y, Shimizu T. The Risk Factors of Hamstring Strain Injury Induced by High-Speed Running. J Sports Sci Med. 2018;17:650-655.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "Sixty-one male track and field athletes were monitored through one season, and 18 hamstring strain injuries from high-speed running were matched to 18 uninjured controls. Hip and knee strength, muscle thickness, range of motion and hamstring tightness were measured before the season, and injury history was obtained by questionnaire. Only a previous hamstring injury was significantly associated with injury.",
  "tldr": "In this small sprinter and jumper squad, a previous hamstring injury was the only factor linked to a sprint-induced hamstring strain. Preseason strength, muscle size and flexibility did not separate injured from uninjured athletes.",
  "methods": "Prospective nested case-control design in one team. Before the season, isokinetic hip and knee strength were measured at 60 deg/s, passive hip and knee range of motion and hamstring tightness by goniometer, and biceps femoris long head and gluteus maximus thickness by ultrasound. Controls were randomly sampled to match injured athletes on history and event.",
  "findings": "Eighteen athletes (29.5%) were injured during 6,258 athlete exposures, an incidence of 2.88 per 1000. Legs with a previous hamstring injury had a higher injury ratio (25.0% vs 10.5%; OR 2.85; p < 0.05). No strength, muscle thickness or tightness measure differed significantly; hip flexion and extension range of motion tended to be larger in injured athletes (p = 0.064 and 0.095).",
  "limitations": "Small sample from one male collegiate team, with age and history matched by design, so selection bias is possible. The tests may lack specificity to sprinting, and the authors note that the study cannot show these factors are unrelated to injury.",
  "practicalImplications": "Athletes with a previous hamstring strain should be treated as higher risk for a sprint-induced recurrence, so injury history belongs in monitoring. The study does not support screening sprinters on preseason isokinetic strength, muscle thickness or flexibility alone.",
  "athleteDev": "Track injury history alongside sprint and jump exposure for sprinters and jumpers, since a previous hamstring strain was the one factor associated with injury here. Preseason strength and flexibility tests did not separate injured from uninjured athletes in this sample.",
  "rtp": "Not a return-to-sport study. It does not show when an athlete can safely return after a hamstring strain and cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria."
 }
}

{

 "sourceFile": "The Role of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) in Neuromuscular Adaptations - Implications for Strength and Power Development—A Review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'The Role of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) in Neuromuscular Adaptations: Implications for Strength and Power Development - A Review' in the text matches the filename; Life 2025, 15, 657.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Review of peer-reviewed studies from 2000 to 2025, found through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and EBSCO, on HIIT and neuromuscular adaptation for strength and power. The text refers to 86 studies from its search and reports that HIIT increases motor unit recruitment and fast-twitch and hybrid IIa fiber activation and improves rate of force development and explosive power, but is less effective than resistance training for maximal strength and hypertrophy.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The authors describe a narrative approach with no inclusion or exclusion framework, yet also call the search systematic. No study counts, screening steps or quality grading are reported, so it is coded as a systematic review under the library's search-method rule, which may overstate its rigour; the operator may recode it as narrative. Many mechanistic claims rest on single cited sources.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read this as evidence that HIIT builds strength and power the way heavy lifting does, when the review itself says HIIT is less effective than resistance training for maximal strength and hypertrophy.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Hung CH, Su CH, Wang D. The Role of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) in Neuromuscular Adaptations: Implications for Strength and Power Development - A Review. Life. 2025;15:657.",
  "doi": "10.3390/life15040657",
  "abstract": "The review examines peer-reviewed studies from 2000 to 2025 on how HIIT affects motor unit recruitment, fiber composition, neuromuscular efficiency, maximal strength, rate of force development, hypertrophy and power. It concludes that HIIT improves neural activation and explosive power, is less effective than resistance training for absolute strength and hypertrophy, and works best combined with resistance or plyometric training.",
  "tldr": "Sprint-based and plyometric HIIT improve explosive power and rate of force development, but HIIT is not a replacement for heavy resistance training for maximal strength. The authors favour combining the two with periodization.",
  "methods": "Narrative synthesis of literature found through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and EBSCO using HIIT and neuromuscular keywords, covering 2000 to 2025, organized by theme. The text refers to 86 studies from its search, with no formal inclusion framework or meta-analysis.",
  "findings": "The authors report that HIIT increases motor unit recruitment and synchronization, with greater fast-twitch activation, shifts toward Type II and hybrid IIa fibers, and improved rate of force development and explosive power. They report HIIT is less effective than traditional resistance training for maximal strength and hypertrophy because it lacks progressive heavy overload.",
  "limitations": "No inclusion criteria, study counts by outcome, or quality grading are reported. The authors note long-term effects are understudied and data for youth and rehabilitation populations are sparse. Mechanistic claims are narrative and not graded for strength of evidence.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use sprint-based or plyometric HIIT to support explosive power and rate of force development, and keep heavy resistance training in the program for maximal strength and muscle size. Schedule HIIT so it does not reduce force output in lifting sessions, and individualize intensity and work-to-rest ratios.",
  "athleteDev": "Use HIIT, especially sprint and plyometric formats, as a time-efficient complement to strength training for explosive power, not as a replacement for heavy lifting. Sequence and periodize it to limit fatigue interference with strength work.",
  "rtp": "Return to play is mentioned only briefly, as early-phase neuromuscular rehabilitation, and injured athletes were not studied. The review cannot be used to set return-to-sport timelines or clearance criteria."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q21",
 "sourceFile": "The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative Tendon Healing - A Scoping Review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative Tendon Healing: A Scoping Review' in the text matches the filename; The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 13(10), 23259671251371300.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 10 non-randomized studies of adults undergoing tendon repair, 8 of them on rotator cuff repair, with sample sizes from 36 to 336,320. Five rotator cuff studies linked vitamin D deficiency to higher retear or revision rates or poorer function, one found no relationship, and the biceps and lateral epicondyle studies reported associations with tendinopathy.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No randomized trials were found, MINORS scores ranged from 4 to 13 of 16 with most studies rated poor, and three studies classified deficiency by ICD codes rather than serum levels. Five studies drew on the same PearlDiver database, so patients overlap. No athletes were sampled, so applicability to athletes is inferred.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the association as evidence that vitamin D supplementation speeds tendon healing, when the review states causality is unproven, the studies are mostly retrospective and low quality, and nearly all data come from rotator cuff repair.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Bouchard MD, Dagher D, Keogh C, Alqahtani M, Khan M. The Role of Vitamin D in Postoperative Tendon Healing: A Scoping Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2025;13(10):23259671251371300.",
  "doi": "10.1177/23259671251371300",
  "abstract": "This scoping review of studies on vitamin D status and tendon healing after surgery found 10 non-randomized studies, most on rotator cuff repair. Vitamin D deficiency was generally associated with delayed healing, higher retear rates and poorer functional recovery, but the evidence was low quality and largely retrospective.",
  "tldr": "Low vitamin D status is associated with poorer healing after rotator cuff repair, but the studies are weak and cannot show that correcting it helps. Vitamin D should not be used as a healing intervention on this evidence alone.",
  "methods": "Systematic search of Embase, Ovid Medline and Emcare to November 2024, following PRISMA-ScR, with two independent screeners and a third to resolve disagreements. Observational studies and RCTs of adults undergoing tendon repair were included, and quality was rated with MINORS. Results were synthesized narratively.",
  "findings": "Ten studies were included: seven retrospective cohorts, one prospective cohort, one matched case-control and one case series. Most studies (8 of 10) examined rotator cuff repair, and five of the rotator cuff studies associated vitamin D deficiency with increased risk of tears, revision surgery, retears or poorer function. Half the studies used the same PearlDiver database.",
  "limitations": "No randomized trials and no prospective data collection in most studies, with low MINORS scores. Vitamin D deficiency was defined by ICD codes in three studies, and patient overlap limits independent conclusions. No athletic populations were studied, and the authors found no research on Achilles, patellar or flexor tendons.",
  "practicalImplications": "The authors suggest clinicians consider individualized vitamin D assessment as part of perioperative care for tendon repair. The evidence does not yet support supplementation to improve healing, and prospective studies and RCTs are needed.",
  "athleteDev": "This review does not show that vitamin D improves performance. Its finding concerns tendon healing after surgery in mostly non-athlete rotator cuff patients, so it should not drive performance supplementation decisions.",
  "rtp": "Not a return-to-sport study. It cannot be used to set rehabilitation timelines or return criteria, or to recommend vitamin D supplementation as part of return-to-play planning."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q22",
 "sourceFile": "The Significance of Body Surface Area to Mass Ratio for Thermal Responses to a Standardized Exercise-Heat Stress Test.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'The Significance of Body Surface Area to Mass Ratio for Thermal Responses to a Standardized Exercise-Heat Stress Test' in the text matches the filename; Med Sci Sports Exerc 57(1):88-93, 2025.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective analysis of heat tolerance test records for 517 Israel Defense Forces soldiers (96% men, mean age 19.8 years) tested after exertional heat illness. Heat-intolerant men had a lower body surface area to mass ratio than heat-tolerant men (248 vs 262 cm2/kg, p < 0.01), and each unit increase in the ratio was associated with an odds ratio of 0.97 for intolerance (95% CI 0.95 to 0.99); the 22 women showed a similar trend that was not statistically significant.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Retrospective registry data from one military testing program, with 96% men, so the female results are underpowered (3 heat-intolerant women). The test does not control for fitness or acclimatization, and the cohort was young soldiers rather than athletes, which the authors say may limit generalizability.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may treat a low body surface area to mass ratio as a screen for heat intolerance or as grounds to restrict return to play, when this is an observational association in one military cohort with a modest odds ratio.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Akavian I, Epstein Y, Rabotin A, Peretz S, Charkoudian N, Ketko I. The Significance of Body Surface Area to Mass Ratio for Thermal Responses to a Standardized Exercise-Heat Stress Test. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025;57(1):88-93.",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000003545",
  "abstract": "A retrospective review of 517 soldiers' heat tolerance test results after exertional heat illness examined whether body surface area to mass ratio relates to heat intolerance. Heat-intolerant men had a lower ratio than heat-tolerant men, and a higher ratio was associated with lower odds of intolerance. The authors suggest the ratio may inform return-to-duty and return-to-play decisions.",
  "tldr": "In men recovering from exertional heat illness, a lower body surface area to mass ratio was linked to failing the heat tolerance test. It is one factor to weigh in return decisions, not a stand-alone screen.",
  "methods": "Retrospective reanalysis of Israel Defense Forces heat tolerance test registry data (2007 to 2021) for 517 soldiers with exertional heat illness. Heat tolerance was defined by a rectal temperature plateau in the second hour of a 2-hour treadmill test at 40 degrees C and 40% relative humidity. Groups were compared with t tests, and logistic regression adjusted for age and modelled with splines.",
  "findings": "In men, heat-intolerant soldiers had lower body surface area to mass ratio than heat-tolerant soldiers (248 vs 262 cm2/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.76). The odds ratio for intolerance was 0.97 per unit increase (95% CI 0.95 to 0.99), with the spline plateauing above about 270 cm2/kg. In women, a similar trend was not statistically significant.",
  "limitations": "Retrospective registry data from a young male military cohort, with no adjustment for fitness or acclimatization. Only 22 women were included, 3 of them heat-intolerant. Heat-intolerant men also weighed more and had higher body fat, and the authors could not rule out other causes such as reduced cardiovascular reserve.",
  "practicalImplications": "When managing return to play after exertional heat illness, a low body surface area to mass ratio may signal a higher chance of failing a heat tolerance test, most clearly in men. The authors recommend deciding return on the test result together with the athlete's history and planned activity, not on the ratio alone.",
  "athleteDev": "A low body surface area to mass ratio is one thing to note when an athlete shows poor heat tolerance on a standard test. It does not show which athletes will perform better in the heat, and the cohort was soldiers rather than athletes.",
  "rtp": "Directly relevant to return to play after exertional heat illness, but the study is observational and does not test whether the ratio predicts safe return. It should not be used alone to clear or hold an athlete, and the authors note that athletic settings with uniforms and different environments may behave differently."
 }
}
